title: I Can Do Better Now
text:
In the summer between my 2nd and 3rd year of university, I took EEB406 at TMU (blg720 by TMU course code) and did some statistical analysis with R. Back then, I had no experience with R and that definitely shows. Since then, I have taken courses where gained some experience with R programming, learned about different data structures and how to manipulate them in R, and have a better understanding of R’s graphical tools. Because of this, I want to go back and re-write some of the work last year to help demonstrate some of the things I learned in 12 months.
Below is an example of something I submitted as part of my EEB406 course project back in early August of 2025 (probably August 4th, plus or minus a day). (Please note that some of these functions are probably given by AI (I knew so little that I had trouble asking about things I didn’t know about) then modified by me. Unfortunately, I am unable to recall what is written by me and what is written by AI.)

title: Zombies!
text:
Introduction:
In my evolutionary medicine course, we had a lecture on zombies where the professor showcased a SIR model for zombism. It was an interesting model, but several modeling assumptions seemed questionable to me. Since I know how mathematical modeling works in ecology and have some experience working with these models (both on paper and using code), I thought it would be a fun project to work on.
First, let me introduce you to the paper. In this paper, they discussed 4 models with different assumptions (their base model, a latent model, a model with quarantine, and a model with treatment). From this, they found that all of humanity will eventually become zombies in every model, and the only way to prevent a zombie outbreak is by killing them all by “strategically destroying them”.
In this project, I will discuss and modify 3 of their models (the base model, the latent infection model, and the model with treatment).

title: Zombies!
text:
Discussion of their paper & models

Model and process overview
Like in the typical SIR model, the authors divide the population into 3, susceptible (the living), the removed class (the dead), and zombies (the living dead). Susceptibles can only become a zombie when they come into contact with a zombie, and the dead are sometimes resurrected as zombies. They assumed that the birth rate is constant, and that zombies move to the removed class once they are defeated by a susceptible (such as through decapitation). This is their first proposed model, as drawn in the diagram below.


Show the code
grViz(" 
digraph zombie_hybrid {
  graph [layout = neato, rankdir = LR, splines = true]

  node [shape = circle, style = filled, fontname = Georgea, fixedsize = true, width= 1]
  
  B [label = '', style = invis, width = 0, pos = '-1,0.2!']
  
  S [label = 'Susceptible', pos = '0,0!']
  R [label = 'Recovered', pos = '4,0!']
  Z [label = 'Zombies', pos = '2,0!']

  B -> S [label = 'π'] # Births
  S -> Z [label = 'βSZ'] # Bitten
  S -> R [label = 'δS', tailport = 's', headport = 's'] # Normal deaths
  R -> Z [label = 'ζR', tailport = 'sw', headport = 'se',  fontsize = '13'] # Resurection
  Z -> R [label = 'αSZ'] # Head got chopped
}
")






From this, it can be seen that the equation should be
\[  S' = \pi - \beta SZ - \delta S \\ Z' = \beta SZ + \zeta R - \alpha SZ \\ R' = \delta S - \zeta R + \alpha SZ \]
\[S' = \pi - \beta SZ - \delta S \] \[ Z' = \beta SZ + \zeta R - \alpha SZ \] \[ R' = \delta S - \zeta R + \alpha SZ \] To check the calculations, I did some of the math via pen and paper as well as used SymPy from python to calculate the equilibrium and stability (via finding the eigenvalues). An example of this is shown below.


Show the code
# https://wasi0013.com/2025/09/20/notes-on-solving-math-equations-in-python-with-sympy-and-todays-llms/
# Their base model
    
# Setting terms
S, I, Z, R, pi, beta, delta, zeta, alpha, rho, c, lamb = symbols('S I Z R pi beta delta zeta alpha rho c lambda')
# Setting the equations
# Note: it is impossible to solve if pi != 0
equation1 = - beta*S*Z + c * Z
equation2 = beta*S*Z - rho * I
equation3 = rho*I + zeta*R - alpha*S*Z - c*Z
equation4 = alpha*S*Z - zeta*R

# Specify which equations to solve and which variables to solve for
# This part of the code gives the equilibrium solutions
solution = solve((equation1, equation2, equation3,equation4), (S, I, Z, R), dict = True) 
equilibrium_solution = "$$" + latex(solution) + "$$"

# Find the Jacobian from the model equations
jacobian_eq_matrix = Matrix([equation1, equation2, equation3,equation4])
jacobian_sym_matrix = Matrix([S, I, Z, R])
Jac = jacobian_eq_matrix.jacobian(jacobian_sym_matrix)
jacobian = "$$" + latex(Jac) + "$$"

# Specify which equilibrium to examine
one_jac = Jac.subs(solution[1]) # Note: For all models, there are only 2 equilibrium
two_jac = Jac.subs(solution[0]) 
jac = one_jac  # ~~~ LOOKIE HERE ~~~
show_jac =  "$$" + latex(jac) + "$$"

char_poly = (jac - lamb * eye(4) ).det() # lambda * identity matrix
characteristic_poly = "$$" + latex(char_poly) + "$$"

eigen_val = solve(char_poly, lamb, dict=True)
eigen_value = "$$" + latex(eigen_val) + "$$"

print(equilibrium_solution)

\[\left[ \left\{ I : 0, \  R : 0, \  Z : 0\right\}, \  \left\{ I : \frac{Z c}{\rho}, \  R : \frac{Z \alpha c}{\beta \zeta}, \  S : \frac{c}{\beta}\right\}\right]\] \[\left[\begin{matrix}- Z \beta & 0 & - S \beta + c & 0\\Z \beta & - \rho & S \beta & 0\\- Z \alpha & \rho & - S \alpha - c & \zeta\\Z \alpha & 0 & S \alpha & - \zeta\end{matrix}\right]\] \[\left[\begin{matrix}- Z \beta & 0 & 0 & 0\\Z \beta & - \rho & c & 0\\- Z \alpha & \rho & - \frac{\alpha c}{\beta} - c & \zeta\\Z \alpha & 0 & \frac{\alpha c}{\beta} & - \zeta\end{matrix}\right]\] \[\left[ \left\{ \lambda : 0\right\}, \  \left\{ \lambda : - Z \beta\right\}, \\  \left\{ \lambda : - \frac{\alpha c + \beta c + \beta \rho + \beta \zeta}{2 \beta} - \frac{\sqrt{\alpha^{2} c^{2} + 2 \alpha \beta c^{2} - 2 \alpha \beta c \rho + 2 \alpha \beta c \zeta + \beta^{2} c^{2} + 2 \beta^{2} c \rho - 2 \beta^{2} c \zeta + \beta^{2} \rho^{2} - 2 \beta^{2} \rho \zeta + \beta^{2} \zeta^{2}}}{2 \beta}\right\}, \\  \left\{ \lambda : - \frac{\alpha c + \beta c + \beta \rho + \beta \zeta}{2 \beta} + \frac{\sqrt{\alpha^{2} c^{2} + 2 \alpha \beta c^{2} - 2 \alpha \beta c \rho + 2 \alpha \beta c \zeta + \beta^{2} c^{2} + 2 \beta^{2} c \rho - 2 \beta^{2} c \zeta + \beta^{2} \rho^{2} - 2 \beta^{2} \rho \zeta + \beta^{2} \zeta^{2}}}{2 \beta}\right\}\right]\]
Reading their paper, it can be seen that \(\pi = 0\) (it would be impossible to solve otherwise) (this is mentioned in their paper). Additionally, they assumed short-term assumptions (meaning no births and no deaths, so \(\pi = 0\) and \(\delta=0\).)


Math Correction
As I was reading through their paper, I noticed that their Jacobian calculations for their treatment model seemed to be wrong. In their paper, they wrote \[\left[\begin{matrix}
\beta Z    &    0   &    - \beta S + c    &    0 \\
\beta Z    &     - \rho    &    \beta S    &    0 \\
- \alpha Z    &    \rho    & - \alpha S - c    &    \zeta \\
\alpha Z    &    0    &    \alpha S    & - \zeta
\end{matrix}\right]\] However, the \(\beta Z\) on the top most right corner should actually be negative. So their calculations for the eigenvalue should really be \[
\begin{aligned}
&(\beta \bar{Z} + \lambda) \det
\begin{bmatrix}
-\rho      &      c      &      0 \\
\rho      &      -\frac{\alpha c}{\beta} - c      &      \zeta \\
0      &      \frac{\alpha c}{\beta}      &      -\zeta
\end{bmatrix} \\
&= -(\beta \bar{Z} + \lambda)(\lambda^3 + \lambda^2(\zeta + \rho + c + \frac{\alpha c}{\beta}) + \lambda(\rho \zeta + c \zeta  + \frac{\rho \alpha c}{\beta}))
\end{aligned}
\] So it is not true that “quadratic expression has only positive coefficients”, so this equilibrium is may in fact be unstable.

title: Zombies!
text:
My Modified Models
There are a couple potential flaws with this model.
For one, even though births (\(\pi\)) and deaths (\(\sigma\)) are generally assumed to be zero when examining how such model behaves in the short term, in major metropolitan areas (such as Toronto or Hong Kong) there are always people being born and dying. In cities with millions of people, the infection may take some time to spread, so it might not be realistic to simulate using such short term assumptions.
Additionally, as one of my classmates pointed out during the lecture, the zombies that had their heads chopped off can still be resurrected from the removed class, which shouldn’t be the case.
Furthermore, the model assumes constant births, which I don’t think is realistic. After all, new humans don’t spontaneously pop into existence, they have to be birthed by another human, so the number of births should be a function of the number of susceptible humans. (In the paper, they assumed \(\pi = 0\), which is why I don’t think their base model was super insightful. After all, if there are no additional living people can be added to the system, it means everyone will become a zombie eventually (as susceptibles can either become zombies or die a natural death. If they die a natural death, they will eventually become zombies).)
Moreover, their models also assumes that everyone who has died can become a zombie. However, depending on condition, not all corpses may be in suitable condition to become zombies (such as fully decomposed or cremated corpses).
Lastly, in their latent model, they assumed that the number of zombies treated (zombies being turned into susceptibles) is solely based on the number of zombies (as denoted by \(cZ\)). I think it is important to point out that it is generally susceptibles who create and administer treatment.
To rectify this, I have made 3 modifications to their model (2 to their every model, the last one only for the treatment model). I assume that

assume \(\pi > 0\) and \(\sigma > 0\)
the group of culled zombies cannot be revived
births is a linear function of the susceptible population
the number of zombies being treated depends on the number of zombies and susceptibles (like the number of zombies being removed)

The reason why I have modeled the removal of the dead as \(\epsilon R\) is because people are not cremated immediately upon their death and it takes time for corpses to break down, which gives them some time to become zombies. While in reality there should be multiple rates, I have combined them into one in this model.

My base model
Graphically, the base model should look like this

  graph [layout = neato, rankdir = LR, splines = true]

  node [shape = circle, style = filled, fontname = Georgea, fixedsize = true, width= 1]

  DZ1 [label = 'Dead\nZombies', style = invis, width = 0, pos = '2.8,1!'] # Zombie removal via susceptibles
  DZ2 [label = 'Dead\nZombies', style = invis, width = 0, pos = '3.2,0.6!'] # Zombie removal by nature
  
  S [label = 'Susceptible', pos = '0,0!']
  R [label = 'Recovered', pos = '4,0!']
  Z [label = 'Zombies', pos = '2,0!']

  B -> S [label = 'πS'] # Births
  S -> Z [label = 'βSZ'] # Bitten
  S -> R [label = 'δS', tailport = 's', headport = 's' ] # Normal deaths
  R -> Z [label = 'ζR'] # Resurection
  Z -> DZ1 [label = 'αSZ'] # Head got chopped off
 # Z -> DZ2 [label = 'γZ', fontsize = '13.8'] # Natural zombie deaths
}")






Leading to the equations
\[S' = \pi S - \beta SZ - \delta S \\
Z' = \beta SZ + \zeta R - \alpha SZ \\
R' = \delta S - \zeta R \]
\[S' = \pi S - \beta SZ - \delta S \] \[ Z' = \beta SZ + \zeta R - \alpha SZ \] \[ R' = \delta S - \zeta R \] \[ \left\{ \lambda : 0\right\}, \  \left\{ \lambda : - \zeta\right\}, \  \left\{ \lambda : - Z \beta - \delta + \pi\right\}\]
Looking at the equations, it can be seen that \(S = 0\) or \(\pi - \beta Z - \delta = 0\) (as shown below). \[\left[ \left\{ R : 0, \  S : 0\right\}, \  \left\{ R : 0, \  S : 0, \  Z : \frac{- \delta + \pi}{\beta}\right\}\right]\] In either case, \(R = S = 0\).
In the first case, Z cannot be determined and the eigenvalues are $ , ,   $. It is unknown if the equilibrium is stable, as stability depends on \(\lambda = -Z \beta - \delta + \pi\). If \(\pi > Z \beta - \delta\), then the equilibrium is unstable. If \(\pi \leqslant Z \beta - \delta\), then this equilibrium is stable.
In the second case, \(Z = \frac{\pi - \delta}{\beta}\). Since both the eigenvalues are negative (\(\left\{ \lambda : 0\right\}, \  \left\{ \lambda : - \zeta\right\}\)), so the equilibrium is stable.
It it important to note that both are doomsday (disease) scenarioes, so we will all become zombies.


My latent infection model
In their paper, the way they modeled the latent infection class is by adding another group (another node). Here, I will do the same. Graphically, the diagram should look like this

  secret1 -> S [label = 'πS'] # Births
  S -> I [label = 'βSZ', fontsize = '13'] # Bitten
  I -> Z [label = 'ρI'] # Turned into zombie
  S -> R [label = 'δS', tailport = 's', headport = 's'] # Normal deaths
  R -> Z [label = 'ζR', tailport = 'w', headport = 'e',  fontsize = '13'] # Resurection
  Z -> DZ1 [label = 'αSZ', headport = 'sw',  fontsize = '12.8'] # Head got chopped
  I -> R [label = 'δI', tailport = 'n', headport = 'n'] # Died midway
}
")






Which gives \[ S' = \pi S - \beta SZ - \delta S \] \[ I' = \beta SZ - \delta I - \rho I \] \[ Z' = \rho I + \zeta R - \alpha SZ \] \[ R' = \delta I + \delta S - \zeta R \]
From the equilibriums, it can be seen that we unfortunately doomed still should there be a zombie outbreak. \[\left[ \left\{ I : 0, \  R : 0, \  S : 0\right\}, \  \left\{ I : 0, \  R : 0, \  S : 0, \  Z : \frac{- \delta + \pi}{\beta}\right\}\right]\]
Similar to the base model, it is unknown if the 1st equilibrium is stable (it again depends on if \(\pi > Z \beta - \delta\)). Since all the eigenvalues for the 2nd equilibrium are negative, it is determined to be stable.

My treatement model
The model where treatment is administered is something like this (note that cZS is dependent on the number of infected and number susceptible).
\[ S' = \pi S + cSZ - \beta SZ - \delta S \] \[ I' = \beta SZ - \delta S - \rho I - \delta I \] \[ Z' = \rho I + \zeta R - cZS - \alpha SZ \] \[ R' = \delta S + \delta I - \zeta R \]
\[\left[ \left\{ I : 0, \  R : 0, \  S : 0\right\}, \  \left\{ I : 0, \  R : 0, \  S : 0, \  Z : \frac{- \delta + \pi}{\beta - c}\right\}\right]\]
\[\left[ \left\{ \lambda : 0\right\}, \  \left\{ \lambda : - \zeta\right\}, \  \left\{ \lambda : - \delta - \rho\right\}, \  \left\{ \lambda : - Z \beta + Z c - \delta + \pi\right\}\right]\]
\[\left[ \left\{ \lambda : 0\right\}, \  \left\{ \lambda : - \zeta\right\}, \  \left\{ \lambda : - \delta - \rho\right\}\right]\]

title: Zombies!
text:
Model Limitations & potential research areas

Model Limitations
However, these models still have a number of flaws. Some are standard to SIR models, some are specific to these models.
Some of the flaws inherent to SIR models are that they do not take into account population structure and they do not account for population density. Population structure is important because only people of certain ages can reproduce, and individuals of different ages may have different survival probabilities during a zombie outbreak. For example, younger people may be more likely to reproduce and be better able to escape zombies. SIR models do not capture such nuances.
Population density also important as it varies across areas. The spread of contact-based diseases depends strongly on how crowded an area is. In areas with higher population density, individuals interact more frequently, aiding in the spread of infectious contact diseases.
The assumption that parameters remain constant over time is another factor that can reduce the accuracy of simple SIR-type models. In reality, many parameters influencing disease spread vary over time.
For one, variations in human behaviour and contact could affect outbreaks likelihood and severity. Such perturbations are not modeled in SIR models.
For example, individuals may alter their behavior and become better at avoiding zombies as an outbreak progresses. Considering that zombism (as portrayed in movies and books) are generally very noticeable and people generally don’t want to die, there are good reasons to believe humanity would get better at killing and avoiding zombies with more time. Another common example where parameters would not be constant is if the impacts of the government and politics were included. In zombie media and in the real world, the government resources and messaging has a large impact the spread of infectious diseases through the populous. These effects are not captured in simple models with fixed parameters.
Actually, in these specific models, the fact that births being modeled as \(\pi S\) with a fixed parameter \(\pi\) means that it is impossible for the model to zombie-free equilibrium. This is because if there were no zombies, then living and the dead can only increase (unless \(\pi=0\), which was my criticism of original paper’s model). Therefore, such models will only ever look at equilibrium where humanity has come to an apocalyptic end.


Potential research areas
There are many modifications that can be made to my proposed models. For example, in a lot of zombie media, zombies zombies are subject to natural decay (as they are literal corpses) and aren’t the brightest bunch, leading them to accidentally offing themselves (such as by drowning or walking into a fire) or to rot away. Future models can examine how a background rate of removal (\(\gamma Z\)) that is unrelated the number of susceptible would affect the model (there should be an equlibrium where some humans may survive, though it is unknown if it is stable or not).
Moreover, it is important to mention that not all corpses are in the right conditions to become zombies. People who were cremated may not be able to become zombies and corpses decompose over time.
Lastly, it may be useful to m

  zeta = seq(from = 0.0001, to = 0.5, length.out = 3),

title: I Can Do Better Now
text:
My current approach (with commentary)

- I think I like to easily modify my inputs to get different outputs.
For example, while I did my project on chloride and nitrate (and since this is based on something I have already submitted, it’s not like this will change), I still wrote it as if I may change it as I think this is how I would write it these days. However, I would still assume that the underlying dataset will is still the same one and wrote accordingly.


- I like to write the modifiable outputs at the top.
As you can see, all the inputs is modified before the for loop, with stops to check that the input is correct. I do this partly out of habbit, and because it makes inputs easier to find and modify.


- I like for loops.
I am aware that there are neater ways of writing this (expand.grid (which should save at least 2 for loops) and purrr::map come to mind), but I didn’t do that.
One reason is because I am less familiar with these methods (I learned about for loops in CSC108). Another would be how I approach coding (and I suspect writing in general). I tend to write as I go, letting structure arise as I write. In terms of coding, I get a rough idea of the steps to complete, and figure out my approach as I code. This lends itself to a lot of for loops, as one needs simply to add another loop rather than figuring out how to re-structure what they have written.
Below is the code (written on the week of September 21st, 2026).

mod.data406 <- data406 |> rename("ec"="spec_cond", "cl"="chloride_a", "f"="fluoride_a", "b"="bromide_a",

  mutate_if(is.character, as.numeric) 
# https://stackoverflow.com/questions/26391921/how-to-convert-entire-dataframe-to-numeric-while-preserving-decimals

compare.ions <- mod.data406 |> select(cl,n) 
# Note: since I did my project of Cl & N, so it's not likely that I will change & use other ions. But still, just in case
things.to.extract <- c("estimate","p.value")
methods <- c("pearson","spearman") 
# I remember that I wasn't sure which method to use. By having "methods" be an input, it makes changing it easier

df <- data.frame(colnames(mod.data406)) |> rename("ions" = "colnames.mod.data406.")

#########

if(all(methods %in% c("pearson","spearman","kendall"))==F){
  stop("We use cor.test here. Please only select from 'pearson', 'spearman', 'kendall'")}
if(all(things.to.extract %in% c("statistic","parameter","p.value","estimate","null.value","alternative","method","data.name","conf.int"))==F){
  stop("We use cor.test here, so you can only call on certain things. Here's the menue:
             -'statistic': Test statistic
             - 'parameter': degrees of freedom
             - 'p.value': likelihood of the result under assuming null is true
             - 'estimate': the correlation coefficient
             - 'null.value': always gives back 0
             - 'alternative': the alternative hypothesis
             - 'method': how the association was measured. You should already know this
             - 'data.name': names of the data being compared. You should already know this
             - 'conf.int': confidence interval")}

for(meth in methods){ 
  
  for (el in 1:length(compare.ions)){ # Note: el & ele are numbers
    results <- vector("list", ncol(mod.data406)) # Create an empty vector to hold results
    
    for (ele in 1:length(colnames(mod.data406))) { 
      # Examine each possible combination & store them in a list
      results[[ele]] <- cor.test(mod.data406[[ele]], compare.ions[[el]], method=meth) 
      # Originally wrote as mod.data406[ele]. ChatGPT corrected it (I could have figured it out myself. I think I was just lazy.)
      }
    for(thing in things.to.extract){
      temp_list <- sapply(results, function(x){x[[thing]]}) # Originally wrote things.to.extract instead of thing here (a dumb mistake)
      # Learned about sapply() from ChatGPT. Still looked up documentation
      # Originally used lapply (as I wanted lists). However, the output, while correct, isn't easily readable, so used sapply
      df <- df |> mutate(temp_list) # Add the values to the data frame
      
      names(df)[names(df) == "temp_list"] <- paste(colnames(compare.ions)[el],meth,thing,sep=" ")
      # Originally was using mutate() but didn't work. ChatGPT suggested this & it works
      # Don't know why I didn't think of this, expecially since this is the method I used above
      # Apparently, rename(corr.list.name = "corr") means "take the existing column "corr" and rename it to
      #             "paste(colnames(compare.ions)[el],meth,thing,sep=" ")"" (quoting ChatGPT)
      # The method above tells R that use the value generated from paste(colnames(compare.ions)[el],meth,thing,sep=" ") as the new name
    
      }
    }  
}
